definition: Emote means to express emotion in an open, theatrical way.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word emote. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know emote should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Contestants on the baking show are coached to emote for the cameras — gasping at ovens, hugging rivals, weeping over sponge cake.
Convey is the quietest — a feeling gets across, perhaps by a single glance; it stops well short of emote, where nothing is left unperformed.
Express lets the feeling show honestly, but it stops short of emote, which stages the feeling for an audience.

Gush means to pour feeling out in words — a flood of thanks, praise, or delight, sincere even when it is over the top. You gush over a gift. Emote does not need words at all: it is feeling staged in the face and body for an audience.

Overact means to push a performance past believability — a stage sin of too much volume and gesture. Emote borrows that sin for daily life: someone who emotes at a podium or a funeral is performing feeling, whether or not any script is involved.

Before microphones reached the movies, acting was a different job.

A silent-film performer had no lines to lean on, so directors ordered them to emote: grief meant a hand clapped to the forehead, joy meant arms thrown wide enough to reach the back row of the theater.
Audiences of the era read the style fluently and loved it.
When sound arrived in 1927, the habit turned overnight from a skill into an embarrassment; critics mocked the flung arms and heaving shoulders as museum pieces.
Actors who could scale their faces down to a murmur kept working, while many stars of the silent era, trained to perform every feeling at full volume, never made another picture.
